import.myskoda.heading: MySkoda app
import.myskoda.intro: Reconciles the charging history from the MySkoda app (charging statistics exported as CSV) with your charging sessions. Start and end SoC and times are corrected, charges without a counterpart are added. You see every change first and pick which to apply.
import.myskoda.help.body: Automatically recorded sessions match the charge that overlaps them or starts at most three hours away. Imports without a time of day (Spritmonitor) match up to four consecutive charges up to their date whose kWh add up to the entry, which also catches entries that combine several charges. Existing kWh, prices, location and odometer stay unchanged. Every change is noted in the session notes. New sessions have no location, provider or odometer and are flagged for review. Anything that can't be matched unambiguously is left alone and listed below as a hint.

settings.myskoda.heading: Automatic Charging Detection (MyŠkoda Public API)
settings.myskoda.description:
A second source, independent of Home Assistant, for automatically detected charging sessions: the server queries the official MyŠkoda Public API itself and creates detected charging sessions (always flagged as "needs review"). The existing Home Assistant push keeps running in parallel, unchanged – the two sources are unaware of each other, so duplicate sessions must be avoided by keeping only one path active per vehicle.

Create an API key at go.skoda.eu/api-keys (open the link on your phone, the MyŠkoda app manages the keys). The key is bound to the vehicles selected when it was created and expires after some time – the expiry date is shown below once a request has been made.

Rate limit: 20 requests per hour per API key, shared across all vehicles and clients. If the Home Assistant integration runs in parallel with the same key, both share this quota – in that case, creating a second key is recommended. The default intervals (20 min idle, 5 min during a charging session) stay comfortably below that.

Accuracy: the start of charging is only noticed on the next poll – with DC fast charging that easily loses a double-digit number of percentage points. By default the SoC of the last poll BEFORE the cable was plugged in is therefore used as the starting value (driving lowers the SoC, so that value can never be below the real starting point). This only applies if that poll is recent enough and the gain was physically possible at the observed charging power – which requires the vehicle's battery capacity to be set. Every detected session gets a note with both raw values so the correction can be traced.

settings.weather.heading: Fetch outside temperature automatically
settings.weather.description: Fills in a charging session's outside temperature when the vehicle did not provide one. What is fetched is the mean of the daytime hours (6–20) across the whole period since the previous charging session – the consumption figure describes exactly that stretch of driving, not the moment of plugging in. This is the basis for the dashboard's “Consumption by outside temperature” analysis. Off by default.
settings.weather.privacy_summary: What is sent to a third-party server
settings.weather.privacy_text: For each charging session, the charging location as a coordinate – rounded to two decimal places, so accurate to roughly 1.1 km – and the period since the previous charging session as a date range are sent to a weather service. This indirectly tells the service which area you charged in; time of day, vehicle, odometer reading and all other data stay here. Without this switch the server never calls an external service on its own.
settings.weather.enabled: Fetch the temperature for new charging sessions automatically
settings.weather.api_url_hint: Leave empty for the public Open-Meteo service. Open-Meteo can also be self-hosted – enter your own address here and nothing leaves your network any more.
settings.weather.backfill_heading: Fill in the temperature for existing charging sessions
settings.weather.backfill_description: Fetches the temperature for every charging session without one that has coordinates (its own or those of its location) – as the mean of the daytime hours (6–20) since the preceding charging session. Existing values – from the vehicle or entered by hand – are left untouched. The trial run really does query the service, but writes nothing.
settings.weather.backfill_refresh: Re-determine values already fetched from the weather service
settings.weather.backfill_refresh_hint: Needed if the backfill ran before version 0.24.1: back then only the value at the start of charging was fetched instead of the mean across the period before it. It was furthest off for charging sessions without a time of day (Spritmonitor imports, all at 00:00) – there it hit the daily minimum. Values from the vehicle or entered by hand stay untouched here as well.

settings.smtp.heading: SMTP Access
settings.smtp.description:
Applies to the whole installation, not per user - the "forgot password" email must be sendable when nobody is signed in. That is why it is admin-only.

Use an app-specific password or a dedicated sender account. The password has to be stored in clear text because SMTP transmits it when authenticating - it could not be recovered from a hash. So the effective protection is not hiding it but limiting what it is worth: an app password can be revoked individually and grants no access to your mailbox. It is never returned through the API, and it is not included in the backup ZIP either.

The base address is the address you use to open this app in your browser. It is needed for the links in the emails and must be set by hand - it must not come from the request, because that would allow links to foreign domains to be injected. Without it, password reset, address confirmation and invitations do not work.

temp.heading: Consumption by outside temperature
temp.help.text: Each dot is one drive: the distance between two charging sessions, plotted against the outside temperature. A drive's temperature is the mean of the values recorded when plugging in before and after it – each is measured at the start of charging, because that is where the drive ends. The green line shows the average per temperature band (weighted by kilometres driven, not per session), the amber one the least-squares fit through all dots. Sessions without a stored temperature are left out – their number appears below the chart. The temperature comes from Home Assistant (service "begin charging session") or is entered by hand when editing a session.
temp.empty: No charging sessions with an outside temperature yet. As soon as Home Assistant sends one (or you enter it by hand), the analysis appears here.
temp.hero.label: more consumption at 0 °C than at 20 °C
temp.hero.detail: {cold} instead of {warm} kWh/100 km per {model} · R² {r2}
temp.model.breakpoint: two lines with the lowest consumption at {at} °C
temp.hero.extrapolated: extrapolated – your data has never seen it this cold
temp.missing: {count} sessions without an outside temperature – not included
tires.description: Record every tire change here: from that date the new set applies until the next entry. The comparison does not pit the raw consumption figures against each other but adjusts for temperature first - otherwise it would only measure that winter tires are driven in winter. What is compared is each set's deviation from the consumption curve over outside temperature (dashboard), converted back to a common reference temperature. A drive with a change somewhere in the middle cannot be attributed to either set and is left out.
tires.hero_detail: Adjusted to {temp} °C; the underlying curve explains r² = {r2} of the spread.
tires.overlap_warning: The sets only overlap by {span} K of temperature. The adjusted figures are therefore mostly an extrapolation into temperatures the respective set never saw.
tires.overlap_missing: The sets were driven in entirely separate temperature ranges, so the adjusted comparison is pure extrapolation - it only becomes meaningful with drives from the changeover months.
tires.excluded: Left out: {without} drives without a tire set, {spanning} drives spanning a change.
tires.empty.no_sets: No tire change recorded yet. The comparison appears once two sets with drives in between exist.
tires.empty.too_few: Too few usable drives per tire set so far. Drives need both a consumption and a temperature value and must lie entirely between two changes.
tires.overview_hint: Only drives that lay entirely on one set are counted - the single drive across a change ran on both and belongs to neither. Kilometres come from the odometer readings of the charging sessions; without them the distance is missing.
tires.km_estimated: Counted from the attributed drives only – the drive across the change is missing. Enter the odometer reading at the change and the figure becomes exact.
tires.getting_started: Record the set that is fitted right now – with the date it was mounted, even if that was a year ago, and the odometer reading from back then if you can still find it (garage invoice, service book). All drives BEFORE that date deliberately stay without a tire set: the app has no idea what was fitted then, and a guessed entry would be worse than none. If you no longer know the exact date, pick a slightly later one rather than one that is too early – guessing too early attributes other sets' drives to this one, guessing too late merely leaves a few drives out. The comparison only starts once the second set is recorded and both have been driven; the overview fills up before that.
tires.form.size_hint: Same size all round? Then the first field is enough. With a staggered fitment it holds the front axle and the one next to it the rear axle.
tires.form.dot_hint: DOT: the last four digits of the DOT number on the sidewall, production week and year (2323 = week 23 of 2023). This gives the tyre age – look more closely from 6 years, replace after 10 years at the latest. If the tyres of one axle have different dates, enter the older one. When the same set is fitted again, the DOT on one of its entries is enough.
tires.form.tread_hint: Tread depth at the change, optional: the lowest measured depth – or all four wheels under "per tyre", then the lowest value counts. The removed set is the one that was on the vehicle until this change. Both measurements get the date and odometer of the change.
tires.tread.hint: Measure in the main grooves at the shallowest point. The legal minimum is 1.6 mm; at least 3 mm is recommended for summer and 4 mm for winter and all-season tyres. At a tyre change both sets can be entered directly in the change form.

settings.fee.heading: Base fees & subscriptions
settings.fee.help_summary: How are base fees accounted for?
settings.fee.help_text: A base fee (e.g. Ionity Powerpass, €15 per month) is split per period across all of this provider's charging sessions in that period, in proportion to the kWh charged. The price paid at the charger stays as it is; the share is shown on top and counts towards total cost, price per kWh and cost per 100 km. A period without any charging session still counts in the statistics. Monthly subscriptions renew on the same day of the month as the start date; an end date ends the subscription (cancellation). For a price change, end the old subscription and add a new one from the new date.
settings.fee.label: Label
sessions.fee_share_tooltip: Share of the provider's base fee (split by kWh), on top of the charger price
sessions.solar_share_tooltip: Share from solar panels or home battery, measured by Home Assistant – the rest came from the grid
battery.heading: Battery and charging losses
battery.help.text: Only charging sessions with a real kWh figure (invoice, wallbox, import) and at least 20 percentage points of SoC gain are used. kWh per percentage point gives the apparent capacity: what charging from 0 to 100 % would cost at the meter. Charging losses are the extra energy compared with the vehicle's nominal battery capacity – with an aged battery they come out slightly too low; the difference between AC and DC is the reliable part. The battery index tracks the apparent capacity per quarter, separately per charging type, relative to the start of your records (100 %). It is not an absolute state of health (SoH), but it shows whether the battery takes less energy over time. Automatically detected sessions without a measured kWh value are left out because their energy is itself estimated from the nominal capacity. Charging losses can only be derived from kWh measured at the charger; whether a provider or a single session was read in the vehicle is set on the provider or in the session form.

battery.health.label: Battery index compared with the start of your records
battery.health.none: Not enough data for a battery capacity history yet (at least three sessions per charging type and two per quarter).

reimbursement.heading: Company car reimbursement
reimbursement.help: For a company car the report lists all home charges – sessions whose provider is set to “Home” – with kWh, where the kWh came from, odometer and reimbursement, plus monthly totals. Charges at work don't count; your employer pays for that power anyway. Reimbursement is either a flat rate per kWh (with a “valid from” date, so a new yearly rate doesn't change past months) or the actual cost of the home charges.
reimbursement.help_estimated: Estimated kWh (state of charge × battery capacity) are not a measurement. They are included but marked in the report and counted at the bottom. The wallbox meter is the more reliable source.

settings.cardata.heading: Charging history from BMW (BMW CarData)
settings.cardata.description:
A third source for automatically recorded charging sessions, for BMW and MINI: the server reads the vehicle's charging history through the official BMW CarData API and creates every completed charging session (always flagged as "needs review"). Unlike MyŠkoda, BMW delivers finished sessions including the energy drawn from the grid – the kWh therefore count as measured (measured at the charger) and are included in the battery index and charging losses.

Setup: 1. In the MyBMW portal (vehicle → BMW CarData), create a client ID and request access to the "CarData API". 2. In the MyBMW app, make sure you are the vehicle's primary user and the charging history is enabled. 3. Enter the client ID here and press "Connect to BMW": a BMW page opens where you confirm the displayed code. The VIN is filled in automatically afterwards if exactly one vehicle is shared.

Quota: 50 requests per day per BMW account, shared with all other clients (e.g. the Home Assistant integration for BMW CarData). The server leaves 10 of them untouched and fetches every 4 hours by default – charging sessions therefore show up with a delay, not immediately.

The login stays valid as long as the server fetches at least every two weeks. Enable only one automatic source per vehicle (Home Assistant, MyŠkoda or BMW), otherwise sessions are duplicated. The provider is set from the charge point operator recognised by BMW only if a provider with exactly that name already exists – otherwise via the charging location as usual.

settings.vwda.heading: VW Group: EU Data Act portal
settings.vwda.description:
Fourth source for automatically recorded charging sessions, for Volkswagen, VW Commercial Vehicles, Audi, Škoda, SEAT, Cupra and Bentley (not Porsche): the server reads the VW Group data portal where every owner can retrieve their vehicle data under the EU Data Act. Like MyŠkoda it only delivers states (cable, charge state, SoC); the server assembles the charging sessions from them. In return, the charged energy comes from the vehicle (measured, without charging losses) instead of the estimate from the SoC.

Setup: 1. Log in to the portal with the brand account (Cupra ID, Škoda account, VW ID etc.) and create a continuous "All Data" request for the vehicle. 2. Enter brand, email address and password of that account here and press "Test connection". The VIN is filled in if exactly one vehicle is shared. 3. Turn on polling.

Good to know: There is no official API, the server logs in like a browser. If VW changes the login page, polling breaks until Lademonitor is updated. If VW asks you to accept new terms, log in once in a browser and accept. The portal delivers new data at most every 15 minutes and only while the car is awake; empty periods of hours are normal. There is no position, you add location and provider when reviewing. The data request expires after about twelve months and has to be renewed in the portal; the server will tell you by email. Enable only one automatic source per vehicle.

Password and VIN are stored encrypted when FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY is set, never shown and not included in backups.

settings.renault.heading: Renault and Dacia: My Renault
settings.renault.description:
Fifth source for automatically recorded charging sessions, for Renault and Dacia with a My Renault account (e.g. Zoe, Megane E-Tech, Scenic E-Tech, Renault 5, Dacia Spring). The server uses the same interface as the My Renault app and the Home Assistant integration renault. It only reports states (cable, charging state, SoC, charging power); the server assembles the charging sessions from them like with MyŠkoda. Energy is estimated from the SoC; odometer, position and outside temperature are taken along if the vehicle provides them.

Setup: 1. Enter country, email address and password of the My Renault account. 2. Press "Log in". If Renault asks for a confirmation code by email, a field for the code appears. 3. Press "Test connection"; the VIN is filled in if the account has exactly one vehicle. 4. Turn polling on.

Good to know: There is no official interface. If Renault changes the login, polling breaks until Lademonitor is adapted. Renault allows about 60 requests per hour and account, shared with the app and Home Assistant. A sleeping vehicle reports its state with a delay. Not every model reports every value (the first-generation Zoe, for example, has no position). Enable only one automatic source per vehicle.

Password, login and VIN are stored encrypted if FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY is set, never shown and not included in the backup.
